Linear algebra. Linear algebra is the branch of mathematics dealing with vectors, matrices, and linear transformations between finite-dimensional spaces. It studies systems of linear equations, the structure of solution spaces, and transformations that preserve linearity. With ubiquitous applications in computer graphics, machine learning, quantum mechanics, and data science, linear algebra is fundamental to modern mathematics and engineering.

A vector is simply an ordered list of numbers, called scalars. Vector spaces are collections of vectors closed under addition and scalar multiplication, forming the foundational structure of linear algebra. A matrix is a rectangular array of numbers that represents a linear transformation and encodes systems of equations. Matrix operations like addition and multiplication express geometric and algebraic relationships in compact form. Every linear transformation can be represented as matrix multiplication.

Among the most important concepts are eigenvalues and eigenvectors. An eigenvector is a special vector that is preserved in direction when the matrix acts on it—it only gets scaled. The scaling factor is called the eigenvalue. These pairs reveal the principal directions of a transformation. The determinant of a square matrix encodes information about the transformation it represents. A zero determinant tells you the transformation is singular and non-invertible; it collapses dimension. Determinants also measure how much a transformation scales volumes.

Systems of linear equations can be written in matrix form as A times x equals b. Linear algebra determines whether this system has solutions, and if so, whether the solution is unique. We solve these using Gaussian elimination, matrix inversion, or more advanced methods. Inner products generalize the dot product to abstract vector spaces, enabling definitions of orthogonality and projection—crucial tools in data analysis and signal processing. Orthogonal matrices and projections are essential throughout applied mathematics.
